html:
Thaana is the script used to write Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives. It appeared in about the 16th or 17th century and, like Arabic, runs from right to left.

Its first letters were made from the Arabic numerals and from local digits, with vowels marked by Arabic-style signs above or below. It replaced Dhives Akuru, an older script descended from Indian Brahmi that was used on copper plates and gravestones since the islands' Buddhist centuries.

Thaana is unlike any other script in the world. It ties Dhivehi, a cousin of Sinhala, to the islands' Muslim culture after the conversion to Islam, and it is taught in every school. In 1976 the government briefly switched official writing to a Latin alphabet, but President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom brought Thaana back in 1978.
